opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I tried to be very upfront about it. Once I had accepted the postdoc offer, I felt it would be unfair to go into conversations with companies pretending I was fully on the market. So when people reached out, and there were quite a few at that time because inference and large model systems were getting really hot, I would usually say at the very beginning: "I've already committed to a postdoc, so I'm not looking to switch right now, but I'm happy to chat and learn what you're working on."

That framing actually made the conversations much more relaxed and, I think, more useful. Neither side was trying to sell anything. They could tell me what problems they were really struggling with in production, and I could share what I was seeing from the open-source side. A lot of those talks turned into collaborations or just long-term friendships, rather than a hiring process.

I also used those conversations as a kind of reality check. In academia it's easy to work on things that feel important to you but don't matter much to people deploying models. Hearing from engineers at companies what their bottlenecks were, whether it was throughput, latency, memory, or just the pain of supporting many different hardware platforms, helped me decide where to focus my own work.

And to be honest, I didn't completely close the door. I told them that if things changed in the future, I'd be glad to reconnect. But I think being clear about my commitment from the start built more trust than keeping options ambiguous would have.

r001.rationale: He says the conversations often turned into collaborations and describes them as useful, relaxed exchanges, communicating that he treated them as a chance to explore collaboration.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was very upfront with everyone. Once I'd accepted the postdoc, I didn't want to play games or keep companies hanging as a backup option, because that's unfair to them and it also doesn't reflect well on you in a small community. The open-source and AI infrastructure world is tiny. Everyone talks.

So when I talked to companies, I'd tell them directly: I've committed to this postdoc, I'm going to honor that commitment, and here's the timeline I'm working with. Then I'd ask what kind of relationship made sense given that. Some people lost interest immediately, which is fine, that saved both of us time. But a surprising number were actually more interested, because they saw someone who keeps their word.

The other thing I did was shift the conversation away from "when can you start" toward "how can we work together in the meantime." With vLLM, for example, a lot of my value to companies wasn't about being a full-time employee. It was about the open-source work itself. So we could talk about collaboration, about what problems they were hitting in deployment, about what features mattered to them. That kind of conversation doesn't require me to sign anything. And frankly, it built relationships that are much deeper than an interview process would have.

I also learned to be clear about what I wanted long-term, not just what I was doing next. Companies appreciate knowing where you're headed. If I said, I want to keep working on inference systems and I care about open source, then they could decide whether that aligned with them, and if it did, the door stayed open. I think a lot of people are afraid that being honest closes doors. In my experience it mostly just filters them.

r001.rationale: He says he shifted conversations toward how they could work together in the meantime, including discussing collaboration and deployment needs.
